As the primary is over, eyes have shifted to the Michigan's U.S. Senate race and governship, as well as various U.S. House races across the state.
Experts at Michigan State University have been following many of these races and issues. They are available to comment on the following topics:

He is an expert on a broad range of topics and campaigns surrounding the 2026 election, including both Michigan and national races and trends.

Marty Jordan is an associate professor in the Department of Political Science and director of the Master of Public Policy (MPP) program at the College of Social Science at Michigan State University. His academic work focuses on policy processes and public administration across U.S. states and localities. He can comment on statewide and local elections as well as federal and state policy issues.

“All voting blocs are consequential, but an increasingly decisive one is the youth vote (ages 18-29). Midterm elections typically see lower participation, yet young voters have significantly increased their civic engagement in recent cycles, reaching roughly 35% turnout in 2018 and 31% in 2022. As we look toward the 2026 midterms in Michigan, a key question is whether this demographic will sustain that momentum and, crucially, which party will secure young voters' support. While younger voters have historically leaned Democratic, the 2024 election cycle signaled a shift. Support for the Democratic ticket notably softened on college campuses across Michigan, including at MSU and U-M, driven by frustrations over economic conditions, high inflation, and the U.S. government’s involvement in the Israel-Hamas war. Whether Generation Z voters remain a reliable Democratic constituency or continue to shift toward new political alignments will be a defining factor in 2026. These voters are grappling with a distinct set of priorities, ranging from the cost of living and housing affordability to the implications of generative AI on the labor market. And many young people are signaling a demand for leadership that moves beyond traditional party orthodoxies.

“Survey respondents are voicing deep-seated concerns over the rising cost of living, the impact of ongoing tariffs on consumer goods, and labor market instability, all set against the backdrop of a prolonged conflict with Iran and heightened anxiety over immigration enforcement. The Trump administration has sought to pivot the narrative toward the ‘One Big Beautiful Bill’ and symbolic politics like the nation’s 250th anniversary. However, it remains unclear whether these communication efforts are gaining traction. Much like the previous administration, the current White House faces an electorate that has grown increasingly impatient, showing little willingness to grant the ‘trial and error’ period that new policy initiatives require to take effect. As we approach November, the central question is whether the 2026 midterms will mirror the 2018 ‘blue wave’ that saw sizable losses for the incumbent party, or the 2022 cycle, where opposition to the repeal of Roe v. Wade blunted those traditional headwinds. Current polling and macroeconomic indicators suggest we are trending toward the former.”

Dante Chinni is a research specialist at the School of Journalism and director of the American Communities Project at the College of Communication Arts and Sciences. He can comment on both the 2026 midterm elections, as well as voter sentiment and patterns across both Michigan and the country.

“The American Communities Project tries to understand what voters living in different kinds of communities are feeling and why. Eight of the project’s 15 community types are represented in Michigan. We are going to be looking at how those different voters are responding to the candidates and issues of the 2026 campaign. Ultimately, the winners and losers in November will be determined by the margins of victory in a set of key counties around the state. Not just Wayne and the Detroit metro area, but smaller counties in the center, west and north of Michigan.”

Eric Juenke is an associate professor in the Department of Political Science and is a faculty member of the Chicano/Latino Studies Program at the College of Social Science. He can comment on Latinx politics, electoral institutions and minority political representation, including for races in Michigan.

“Get ready to see some political ads this fall. Michigan will once again be in the national spotlight for control of Congress. Not only will our Senate race be competitive and influential for control of the Senate, but our local House district race, featuring incumbent Tom Barrett (R) and a group of Democratic challengers will also be key to which party controls the House. Because we already know the Republican candidates —Mike Rogers is the likely GOP Senate nominee — I’ll be watching the Democratic primary elections in August. These races reflect the national storyline for Democrats, with establishment candidates like Haley Stevens taking on progressive challengers like Abdul El-Sayed for the Senate seat.

“In MSU’s House District 7, the progressive candidate is William Lawrence, and the establishment candidates are Bridget Brink and Matt Maasdam. After the primaries, I’ll be watching closely to see if Democrats are able to rally around candidates that are not preferred by many in their own party. Will the GOP survive a backlash midterm year with an unpopular incumbent president because the Democrats are too divided? Or will none of this matter in Michigan because the midterm wave is going to be too large for the GOP to overcome? This is the national story of the midterms, with so much riding on control of Congress for the next two years. We will have a front row seat here in Michigan with the nation’s eyes glued to our results in November.”

Jeremy Orr is an adjunct professor at the Michigan State University College of Law and an attorney specializing in environmental and civil rights law. He can comment on Michigan’s elections with regard to environmental policy.

Governor race: Flooding and climate infrastructure policy

“The 2026 governor’s race is also going to be shaped by the reality that climate change is no longer an abstract issue for Michigan communities. People are experiencing it directly through flooding, stronger storms, failing infrastructure, power outages, and the growing strain on systems that were never built for this level of extreme weather. Across the state, residents are seeing flooded basements, overwhelmed drainage systems, damaged roads and aging water infrastructure struggling to keep up. What used to be talked about mostly as a global climate issue is now showing up as a very local governance and quality of life issue.

“That means the next governor is going to face increasing pressure to prioritize climate resilience and infrastructure modernization as core parts of governing. This is about more than environmental policy. It is about housing, public health, affordability, emergency preparedness, and whether communities actually have infrastructure that can safely support them in the years ahead. Michigan has an opportunity to lead with a people-centered approach to climate resilience, but doing that will require long-term investment, coordination and a willingness to treat these issues with the urgency they now demand.”
16-year constitutional convention vote and ballot proposals

Quinn Yeargain, 1855 Professor of the Law of Democracy, who is also an associate professor at the Michigan State University College of Law, can provide insights on the topic of constitutional conventions, which occur every 16 years in Michigan — and it happens to be on the 2026 ballot.

“The first Michigan Constitution, which was drafted in 1835, allowed the legislature to call a constitutional convention if voters agreed to do so. When the constitution was rewritten in 1850, delegates added in the current provision, which requires that the question of whether to hold a convention be put to voters every 16 years. The delegates debated what the appropriate amount of time was — the original draft of the constitution proposed an election every 15 years, and some delegates wanted to have an election every 10 years — and ultimately settled on 16. The provision endured in the 1908 and 1963 constitutions.

“Surveys have shown that only a bare majority of voters are aware that their state has a constitution, and voters don’t have a lot of knowledge about what their constitution contains. As a result, it’s understandable that they don’t have very strong feelings about documents that they don’t know very much about. Though state constitutions have increased in salience in the last decade — and especially in the last five years — they’re still not something that most voters are familiar with. And the prospect of authorizing politicians to totally rewrite the state’s governing document, with no guarantee of what would stay from the current constitution, might be a frightening prospect. We’ll see how voters feel, but the Michigan Constitution has held up really well — and has proven adaptable in changing times.”

Erik Nordman is an associate professor in the Department of Agricultural, Food and Resource Economics at the College of Agriculture and Natural Resources, where he also directs the Institute of Public Utilities at Michigan State University. He can discuss the Michigan Utility and Government Contractor Campaign Finance Regulations Initiative as it received approval for the November ballot.

“Michigan’s electric and gas utilities are allowed to have a near-monopoly on the sale of their services within their defined territories. In return, they agree to have their prices and service quality regulated by the Michigan Public Service Commission. They must also follow statutes set by the Michigan legislature. Should the utilities be able to contribute to the political campaigns of legislator and the governor, who appoints the public service commissioners? That is the question being put to Michigan voters in a ballot proposal this year. Specifically, the ballot initiative would prohibit the regulated utilities from contributing money to the political campaigns of state officeholders and political party committees. It also would prohibit companies that have large contracts ($250,000) or more from contributing to political campaigns of candidates for state or local offices in the jurisdiction in which they work. The bill’s proponents are concerned about the utilities ‘capturing’ their regulators with campaign funds. Opponents of the ballot initiative say such restrictions are unconstitutional limitations on free speech. The state canvassers will meet on July 24, 2026, to determine the petition’s sufficiency and the ballot’s 100-word summary.”

Jeremy Orr is an adjunct professor at the Michigan State University College of Law and an attorney specializing in environmental and civil rights law. He can also comment on the Michigan Utility and Government Contractor Campaign Finance Regulations Initiative as it received approval for the November ballot.

"Michigan families deserve an energy system that works for them, not one where monopoly utilities can use their immense financial power to influence the very elected officials responsible for holding them accountable. Our utilities are government-granted monopolies, and with that privilege should come even greater responsibility to make sure our grid is clean, safe, and affordable.

"At a time when Michigan is making critical decisions about energy affordability, grid reliability, and the transition to clean energy, the public needs to know those decisions are being made in the public interest not for their bottom line. On the surface, the MOP UP Michigan ballot initiative is about getting monopoly money out of our politics and restoring trust in our state government. But, if successful, our political system will be much better positioned to regulate utilities, lower the cost of healthcare, and tackle some of our state’s toughest challenges."

Madeline Mavrogordato is the director of the Education Policy Innovation Collaborative, or EPIC, at the College of Education, where she is also a professor in the Department of Educational Administration. She can discuss the importance of reading and literacy along with the associated challenges learners face.

“Michigan voters have watched our state’s literacy performance steadily decline over the past two decades. In 2002, only 13 states had fourth grade reading proficiency rates that were statistically higher than Michigan’s; today, that number has grown to 31. The leaders and policymakers Michigan voters elect this November will determine whether that trend continues or begins to reverse. Strong literacy outcomes are the foundation for student success, a competitive workforce and thriving communities, making literacy one of the most consequential issues facing our state and a key issue for Michigan voters this election.”

Jason Burns is a research specialist with the Education Policy Innovation Collaborative, or EPIC, at the College of Education, where his focus is supporting EPIC’s portfolio of research on Michigan’s teacher workforce. He can discuss the importance of education and its funding.

“Our public opinion research shows that K-12 education funding is a significant priority for Michigan residents. Among the major areas of state spending we examined, including roads and bridges and healthcare, more Michiganders favored increasing funding for K-12 education than for any other area. That preference aligns with a large and growing body of research showing that school funding matters for student outcomes. Together, the evidence suggests that education funding is important to Michiganders and has meaningful consequences for students and schools.”

Several communities have passed moratoria on new data center developments as they explore ways to protect their residents while accommodating the new facilities. In July, Governor Whitmer issued a Michigan Affordable and Responsible Growth Action Plan for data centers. The plan encourages the legislature to pass laws that enforce the ratepayer protections already in place with the Michigan Public Service Commission. The plan also includes a voluntary commitment for data center owners to protect their host communities and support local economies.”
